name: Designing Experiments and Using Simulations
title: Designing Experiments and Using Simulations
answer: This idea uses a school configured AI tool as a coach for three science tasks: helping students design fair experiments, guiding them through simulations of things that would be dangerous, expensive or impossible in a real lab, and generating short misconception probes so teachers can see what students actually believe before a lesson. It matters because designing a good experiment is one of the hardest skills in science, and students often test too many things at once, forget a control, or choose a measure that will not answer their question. The AI asks the questions a good teacher would ask, while the student still does the designing and the teacher still checks the accuracy of every probe.

sections.body: Designing a good experiment is one of the hardest skills in science, and students often test too many things at once, forget a control, or choose a measure that will not answer their question. A school configured tool can act as a coach in that moment, asking what the student will change, what they will keep the same, and how they will know whether their idea was right. The student remains the designer, and the coach supplies the questions a good teacher would ask. Simulations extend the same coaching to work that would be dangerous, expensive or impossible in a real lab, letting a student change gravity on a virtual planet or run a chemical reaction many times in a few minutes. Misconception probes address a different problem, which is that a teacher cannot plan well without knowing what students really believe.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, the coaching appears at the point where a student is planning an investigation: the tool asks what will change, what will stay the same, and how the student will know if the idea was right, and the student then writes the design. During simulation work the AI asks what the student predicts before each run and what they notice after, and the prediction step is what turns clicking into thinking. For planning, a teacher can ask an AI tool for short questions built to reveal common misunderstandings, such as believing that heavier objects fall faster, then have students answer before the lesson and use the results to plan. The text does not assign these practices to particular grade bands, so schools adapt the same three moves, experiment design coaching, prediction before simulation runs, and pre lesson probes, to the level of science their students are doing.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it does state is a set of observations about how students typically struggle, that they test too many things at once, forget a control, or choose a measure that will not answer their question, along with a claim about why the prediction step matters, because it turns clicking into thinking. The misconception probe is presented as a planning aid whose value depends on the teacher checking each question for accuracy. Beyond that, the chapter makes no claim about measured gains in learning.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits sit with the people, not the tool. The student designs the experiment and the AI only asks the questions a good teacher would ask, so the intellectual work of framing a fair test stays with the learner. A poorly worded misconception probe can plant the very misconception it was meant to find, which is why the teacher checks every question for accuracy before using it. The teacher also decides how to use the probe results to plan, and the prediction step in a simulation only does its work if the student is asked to commit to a prediction before running anything. Simulations are chosen for what would be dangerous, expensive or impossible in a real lab, not as a replacement for the lab itself.
